newsitem.title: JORDAN: Chirac, Hussein worried over Mideast peace outlook.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Hussein worried over Mideast peace outlook.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and Jordan's King Hussein say they are concerned about the faltering Middle East peace process and worried that extremists may gain the upper hand.

Chirac arrived in Jordan on Wednesday from the Palestinian territories where he received a hero's welcome after a tense two days in Israel, where his visit was marred by heavy security, diplomatic incidents, media hostility and public indifference.

After talks with King Hussein on Wednesday night, Chirac was quoted by a spokesman as saying: "We share the same feeling about the evolution of the region and the peace process. We share the same anxiety."

A senior French official said Chirac's prevailing impression of his visits to Syria, Israel, the Palestinian territories and Jordan was that the peace process was in crisis and the forces of evil might prevail.

King Hussein struck a similar note of gloom in an interview with the international Arabic newspaper al-Hayat published on the day Israel marked the first anniversary according to the Jewish calendar of the assassination of peace-making prime minister Yitzhak Rabin by a Jewish rightist.
"Since the assassination of Rabin, we started feeling that the extremists are dictating their will on the arena," he said.
"What is dangerous is to reach a point where people lose hope and then deterioration could be accelerated. It is easy to destroy but difficult to construct," the king said.
King Hussein backed Chirac's drive to increase French and European political influence on Arab-Israeli peace negotiations, provided it was in harmony with U.S. mediation efforts.

On his Middle East tour, due to be concluded with a 20-hour visit to Lebanon from Thursday night and a stopover in Cairo, Chirac has called for the European Union to co-sponsor the peace process, saying Europe can help restore confidence in the area.

Hours after he left the Gaza Strip, Israel imposed a total closure of the Palestinian territories in what it said was a measure to prevent possible attacks on the anniversary of the assassination of Palestinian Islamic Jihad leader Fathi Shqaqi in Malta by suspected Israeli agents.

In contrast to Chirac's vibrant plea in Israel and Ramallah for a Palestinian state, King Hussein avoided any mention of a state in his interview, saying only that the Palestinians must have the right to live on their own soil.
Jordan ruled the West Bank until the 1967 Middle East War, when Israel captured the area and the Jordanian-held eastern sector of Jerusalem.
However, the French official said Chirac did not gain the impression that Jordan viewed the emergence of a Palestinian state as a threat to its Hashemite monarchy.

Chirac used his visit to Jordan to appeal for international action to ease the plight of the civilian population of neighbouring Iraq. He noted that the U.N. embargo on Iraq, imposed after President Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, continued to harm the Jordanian economy.
"I hope that once it has fulfilled all the obligations set by the U.N. Security Council, that great country can return to its rightful place in the community of nations," said Chirac.
"But as of now, however, we must prevent the humanitarian plight of the Iraqi people from getting worse. This is why France advocates the rapid implementation of Resolution 986."

That resolution would enable Baghdad to sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and medicines. A deal to implement the policy, struck in May, has been blocked by the United States since a clash with Iraq in September over Baghdad's intervention in fighting between rival Kurdish factions in northern Iraq.
